steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- What AC 20-152A is
  - title: Development Assurance for Airborne Electronic Hardware
  - names RTCA standard DO-254: "an acceptable means, but not the only means" to get FAA approval of electronic hardware in FAA airspace
  - Revision A released 2022: effectively complete rewrite, big expansion
  - now important instrument: completes/updates some guidance, gives applicants clarifications + additional info on the standard
  - Revision A = "a stop-gap measure" until DO-254A (rising complexity of COTs hardware; make explicit much reduced effort for simple hardware and DAL D hardware)
  - replaces AC 20-152, CAST-27, EASA CM SWCEH-001
- Scope before/after
  - initially DO-254 read as only for complex custom micro-coded components, IDAL A, B, C
  - DO-254 guidance on simple hardware etc. needed clarification
  - 2022 Rev A: AC 20-152() and DO-254 apply to type certification of all electronic hardware aspects of airborne systems, incl. all simple hardware at greatly reduced effort
- Additional objectives
  - 29 objectives on top of DO-254
  - applicants following DO-254 under AC 20-152A must accomplish all that apply to their hardware
- Devices
  - COTS microcontrollers excluded (see AC 20-115()/DO-178C)
  - covers complex custom micro-coded components: FPGA, PLD, ASIC
  - esp. where correctness/safety can't be verified by testing alone -> methodical design assurance (DO-254, DAL A through DAL C)
  - simple devices: verifiable by testing alone; FAA may agree methodical design assurance unnecessary
## Relief for DAL D
- applicant following DO-254 need not apply this AC; FAA does not expect to examine life cycle data
- alternative design practices for DAL D (permitted by AC) -> FAA will review data
## Application to circuit board assemblies
- one new objective: DO-254 applies to circuit board assemblies (CBA) contributing to DAL A/B/C functions
## Relationship to FAA Order 8110.105
- companion AC 00-72, Best Practices for Airborne Electronic Hardware Design Assurance Using EUROCAE ED-80() and RTCA DO-254()
- chapters 3 through 6 of Order 8110.105A removed in Revision B (2024) to avoid duplication/conflict
- removed sections had been an expedient solution to concerns of authorities and applicants
- reason: FAA now avoids internal Orders and Notices for guidance to applicants
- AC 20-152A: new guidance closing gaps in DO-254; AC 00-72: "additional information" on some new objectives

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
AC 20-152A is an FAA Advisory Circular with the title Development Assurance for Airborne Electronic Hardware. It identifies DO-254, which is a standard published by RTCA, as defining "an acceptable means, but not the only means" to get FAA approval of electronic hardware that is used within the airspace that is subject to FAA authority. Revision A was released in 2022 and it was effectively a complete rewrite and a big expansion of the circular. Because of this the Advisory Circular is now a very important instrument, it completes and updates some of the existing guidance and it gives applicants clarifications and additional information on the standard. Revision A was developed and released as "a stop-gap measure" until DO-254A can be released. DO-254A is supposed to address the rapidly increasing complexity of COTs hardware and also to make explicit that the assurance effort needed for simple hardware and DAL D hardware is greatly reduced. The revision replaces AC 20-152, CAST-27, and EASA CM SWCEH-001.

At first DO-254 was commonly interpreted as only applying to complex custom micro-coded components in aircraft systems that had Item Design Assurance Levels (IDAL) of A, B, or C. But the guidance in DO-254 on simple electronic hardware and some other topics needed some clarification. Revision A of this AC in 2022 clarified that AC 20-152() and DO-254 apply to the type certification of all the electronic hardware aspects of airborne systems. This includes all simple electronic hardware, at greatly reduced effort.

- 29 additional objectives beyond DO-254; applicants following DO-254 under AC 20-152A must do all that apply to their hardware
- COTS microcontrollers excluded (see AC 20-115()/DO-178C)
- covers FPGA, PLD, ASIC, esp. where correctness/safety can't be verified by testing alone -> methodical design assurance (DO-254, DAL A through DAL C)
- simple devices: verifiable by testing alone, FAA may agree methodical design assurance unnecessary

## Relief for DAL D
- following DO-254 -> no need to apply AC; FAA does not expect to examine life cycle data
- alternative design practices (permitted) -> FAA reviews data

## Application to circuit board assemblies
- new objective: DO-254 applies to CBA contributing to DAL A/B/C functions

## Relationship to FAA Order 8110.105
- companion AC 00-72, Best Practices for Airborne Electronic Hardware Design Assurance Using EUROCAE ED-80() and RTCA DO-254()
- chapters 3 through 6 of Order 8110.105A removed in Revision B (2024), avoid duplication/conflict
- had been expedient solution to concerns of authorities and applicants
- FAA now avoids internal Orders and Notices for guidance
- AC 20-152A closes gaps in DO-254; AC 00-72 "additional information" on some new objectives

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
AC 20-152A is an FAA Advisory Circular with the title Development Assurance for Airborne Electronic Hardware. It identifies DO-254, which is a standard published by RTCA, as defining "an acceptable means, but not the only means" to get FAA approval of electronic hardware that is used within the airspace that is subject to FAA authority. Revision A was released in 2022 and it was effectively a complete rewrite and a big expansion of the circular. Because of this the Advisory Circular is now a very important instrument, it completes and updates some of the existing guidance and it gives applicants clarifications and additional information on the standard. Revision A was developed and released as "a stop-gap measure" until DO-254A can be released. DO-254A is supposed to address the rapidly increasing complexity of COTs hardware and also to make explicit that the assurance effort needed for simple hardware and DAL D hardware is greatly reduced. The revision replaces AC 20-152, CAST-27, and EASA CM SWCEH-001.

At first DO-254 was commonly interpreted as only applying to complex custom micro-coded components in aircraft systems that had Item Design Assurance Levels (IDAL) of A, B, or C. But the guidance in DO-254 on simple electronic hardware and some other topics needed some clarification. Revision A of this AC in 2022 clarified that AC 20-152() and DO-254 apply to the type certification of all the electronic hardware aspects of airborne systems. This includes all simple electronic hardware, at greatly reduced effort.

Revision A also defines 29 objectives that are additional to the ones identified in DO-254. If applicants choose to follow DO-254 under the authority of AC 20-152A, they must also accomplish all of these additional objectives that apply to their particular hardware.

COTS microcontrollers are specifically excluded (see AC 20-115()/DO-178C). The advisory addresses complex custom micro-coded components, which include field programmable gate arrays (FPGA), programmable logic devices (PLD), and application-specific integrated circuits (ASIC). It is mainly about cases where correctness and safety cannot be verified through testing alone, so that methodical design assurance processes are necessary, such as the processes in DO-254 for DAL A through DAL C. Simple devices are devices that can be verified with testing alone, so the FAA may agree that methodical design assurance is unnecessary for them.

## Relief for DAL D

For DAL D hardware, the applicant does not need to apply this advisory circular as long as they follow DO-254, because the FAA does not expect to examine the life cycle data. But if the applicant chooses to follow alternative design practices for DAL D hardware (which this AC permits) then the FAA will review the data.

## Application to circuit board assemblies

AC 20-152A has one new objective that explicitly states that DO-254 applies to circuit board assemblies (CBA) that contribute to hardware DAL A, DAL B, or DAL C functions.

## Relationship to FAA Order 8110.105

AC 20-152A was expanded and released together with a companion AC, AC 00-72, Best Practices for Airborne Electronic Hardware Design Assurance Using EUROCAE ED-80() and RTCA DO-254(). After that, chapters 3 through 6 of FAA Order 8110.105A were removed in a Revision B, released in 2024, so that there would not be any duplication or conflict with the new ACs. The removed sections had been published as an expedient solution to concerns of both the authorities and the applicants. They were removed because the FAA now avoids using internal FAA Orders and Notices to give guidance and clarifications to applicants. Where the two new ACs replace material in Order 8110.105, AC 20-152A gives new guidance to close gaps in DO-254, and AC 00-72 gives "additional information" on some of the new objectives in AC 20-152A.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The Advisory Circular AC 20-152A, Development Assurance for Airborne Electronic Hardware, identifies the RTCA-published standard DO-254 as defining "an acceptable means, but not the only means" to obtain FAA approval of electronic hardware used within the airspace subject to FAA authority. With the 2022 release of Revision A (effectively a complete rewrite and a large expansion), this Advisory Circular becomes a very important instrument for completing and updating some DO-245 guidance and for giving applicants clarifications and additional information on that standard.[1,2] Revision A was developed and released as "a stop-gap measure" until DO-254A can be released to address the rapidly increasing complexity of COTs hardware and to make explicit the greatly reduced assurance effort needed for simple hardware and DAL D hardware. This revision replaces AC 20-152, CAST-27, and EASA CM SWCEH-001.[3]

Initially, DO-254 was commonly interpreted as applying only to complex custom micro-coded components within aircraft systems with Item Design Assurance Levels (IDAL) of A, B, or C.[4,5] However, the DO-254 guidance on simple electronic hardware and some other topics needed clarification. In 2022, Revision A of this AC clarified that AC 20-152() and DO-254 apply to the type certification of all electronic hardware aspects of airborne systems, including all simple electronic hardware, at greatly reduced effort.

Revision A also defines 29 objectives in addition to those identified in DO-254. Applicants who choose to follow DO-254 under the authority of AC 20-152A must also accomplish all of these additional objectives that apply to their particular hardware.[6]

Specifically excluding COTS microcontrollers[7] (see AC 20-115()/DO-178C), this advisory addresses complex custom micro-coded components, including field programmable gate arrays (FPGA), programmable logic devices (PLD), and application-specific integrated circuits (ASIC), particularly where correctness and safety cannot be verified through testing alone and methodical design assurance processes such as those defined in DO-254 for DAL A through DAL C are therefore necessary.[8] Simple devices are those verifiable with testing alone, such that the FAA may agree that methodical design assurance is unnecessary.

## Relief for DAL D

For DAL D hardware, as long as the applicant follows DO-254, the applicant does not need to apply this advisory circular, since the FAA does not expect to examine the life cycle data.[5,7] However, if the applicant chooses to follow alternative design practices for DAL D hardware (as this AC permits), the FAA will review the data.[9]

## Application to circuit board assemblies

One new objective in AC 20-152A explicitly states that DO-254 applies to circuit board assemblies (CBA) that contribute to hardware DAL A, DAL B, or DAL C functions.[10]

## Relationship to FAA Order 8110.105

With the release of the expanded AC 20-152A and its companion AC 00-72, Best Practices for Airborne Electronic Hardware Design Assurance Using EUROCAE ED-80() and RTCA DO-254(), chapters 3 through 6 of FAA Order 8110.105A were removed in a Revision B, released in 2024, to eliminate any duplication or conflict with the new ACs. The removed sections had been published as an expedient solution to the concerns of both authorities and applicants. They were removed because the FAA now avoids using internal FAA Orders and Notices to provide guidance and clarifications to applicants. Where the two new ACs replace material in Order 8110.105, AC 20-152A provides new guidance to close gaps in DO-254, while AC 00-72 provides "additional information" on some of the new objectives in AC 20-152A.[11,1]
